question: What is autoregressive decoding?
choices: One token at a time, each conditioned on the ones before it
All tokens of the sequence at once, from the prompt alone
Re-running the model on its output until it stops changing
explanation: A language model gives a distribution over the next token given a prefix; decoding appends one sampled token and repeats, so the steps are inherently sequential.

title: A decode step
question: What is one decode step of a transformer?
choices: One prompt token being written into the KV cache
One forward pass yielding the next-token distribution
One layer of the model applied to the whole sequence
explanation: Each step runs the full model over the current position (with the cached prefix) and ends with a distribution from which one token is sampled.

question: What is memory-bound decoding?
choices: Steps that stop because the KV cache has filled GPU memory
Steps whose time is set by reading the weights from memory
Steps whose time is set by the arithmetic of the matmuls
explanation: At small batch a step reads every weight once to do very little arithmetic per weight, so memory bandwidth, not compute, bounds its time; compute-bound is the opposite regime.

question: What is compute-bound decoding?
choices: Steps limited by how fast the sampler can draw tokens
Steps that wait on the CPU to prepare the next batch
Steps whose time is set by arithmetic, not by weight reads
explanation: With a large batch the same weights serve many positions, the arithmetic per weight read grows, and the arithmetic units become the bottleneck.

question: What is the acceptance rate, alpha?
choices: The share of iterations in which every guess survives
The fraction of the vocabulary the draft and target agree on
The probability that the target accepts one draft guess
explanation: Alpha is the expected probability that a draft token passes the acceptance test; it depends on how close the draft's distribution is to the target's.

title: Cost coefficient
question: What is the cost coefficient, c?
choices: The fraction of tokens that the draft gets wrong
The number of draft parameters divided by target parameters
The time of one draft step as a fraction of one target step
explanation: The paper measures draft cost in target-step units; c near zero means a nearly free draft, c near one a draft as slow as the target.

title: Exact (lossless) decoding
question: What does it mean that speculative decoding is exact?
choices: The draft and the target always produce the same token
The output text is identical to the small model's
Each output token has exactly the target's distribution
explanation: Nothing about quality is traded: a sequence decoded speculatively is distributed as if the target had decoded it alone, which is proved, not measured.

question: What is the residual distribution used when a guess is rejected?
choices: The target's distribution with the rejected token removed
Target minus draft probabilities, clipped at zero, renormalized
The average of the target's and the draft's distributions
explanation: Written norm(max(0, p - q)), it holds exactly the probability mass the target wanted that the draft did not propose.

title: One token per pass
context: Decoding a transformer is autoregressive: each new token needs a full forward pass over the prefix, and that pass must read every weight from memory. At the batch sizes of interactive serving a step moves tens of gigabytes of weights to produce one token, so the step is bound by memory bandwidth and the arithmetic units sit mostly idle. A smaller model is faster but changes the output. Many tokens in a sequence are easy: a far smaller model predicts them just as the large one would; a few are hard. Plain decoding does not exploit the difference: every token, easy or hard, costs one full pass of the large model.

question: Why does a large model's decode step produce only one token, when the hardware could do far more arithmetic in that time?
choices: The KV cache must be rewritten before another token can start
Each token depends on the previous one, so steps cannot overlap
The sampler needs the full vocabulary sorted before each token
explanation: Autoregressive decoding is sequential by definition: the next input is the token just produced, so the model is called once per token however idle the arithmetic units are.

choices: Multiplying the prefix's activations by the weights
Sorting the vocabulary to sample the next token
Streaming the weights from memory into the chips
explanation: One token's worth of arithmetic is tiny next to reading every weight once, so the step is memory-bound; that idle arithmetic is what speculative decoding spends.

title: Why not the small model
question: A small model predicts most tokens exactly as the large one would. Why not simply serve the small model?
choices: A smaller model is no faster once it fits in memory
The hard tokens are where its answers differ and matter
Small models cannot run at batch size one
explanation: Quality lives in the minority of hard tokens; the paper's goal is to keep the large model's output exactly while paying the large model's price only where it is needed.

choices: Arithmetic: the chips could handle more positions per pass
Bandwidth: the weights could be streamed faster
The KV cache, which is read only at the final layer
explanation: Running the same weights over several positions at once costs little more than one position while the weights are the bottleneck, which is exactly the room the method uses.

title: One pass, many positions
context: Speculative decoding keeps the large target model and adds a cheap approximation model, the draft, which shares the target's vocabulary. Each iteration the draft runs autoregressively a few times, gamma times, producing gamma guessed tokens. The target then runs once over the prefix plus all gamma guesses in parallel, which yields its next-token distribution at every one of those positions in a single pass. The guesses are checked left to right against the target's distributions; the first rejected guess is replaced by a token drawn from the target, and everything after it is discarded. If every guess survives, one more token comes from the target's last distribution. So an iteration costs one target pass plus gamma cheap draft steps and yields between one and gamma plus one tokens.

question: Why does the target's single pass over gamma plus one positions cost about the same as a pass over one position?
choices: The draft already computed most of the activations
The step is memory-bound; the same weights serve every position
Positions after the first reuse the first one's attention
explanation: Reading the weights dominates the step, and they are read once however many positions are in the batch, so verifying several guesses is nearly free until the arithmetic becomes the bottleneck.

title: Why the draft runs step by step
question: Why must the draft produce its gamma guesses one after another rather than in a single parallel pass?
choices: Parallel drafting would need the target's KV cache
The acceptance test needs the tokens in order
Each guess conditions on the guess before it
explanation: The draft is an ordinary autoregressive model proposing a continuation, so guess k is sampled given guesses one to k minus one; only the target's check is parallel.

title: Always at least one token
question: Why does an iteration always make progress, even when the draft's very first guess is rejected?
choices: The rejection itself yields a token drawn from the target
A failed iteration is retried with a smaller gamma
The first guess is accepted by rule, whatever the target says
explanation: On rejection the method samples the replacement from the target's adjusted distribution at that position, so the worst case is one target-quality token per iteration, the same as plain decoding.

title: The extra token
question: All gamma guesses were accepted. Why can the iteration add one more token at no extra cost?
choices: The target's pass already covered one position past the guesses
Accepted guesses prove the draft right, so it gets one more
The draft runs one extra step while the target finishes
explanation: The target was run on gamma plus one positions, the last being the position after the final guess, so its distribution there is available and one token is sampled from it directly.

title: Nothing is retrained
question: What makes this usable with an existing large model today?
choices: The target is distilled once into the draft
The target needs a short fine-tune on the draft's output
The target is unchanged; only its sampling loop changes
explanation: The method wraps the target's forward pass and sampling; the draft can be any existing smaller model with the same vocabulary, so no training is needed on either side.

title: Why thin rather than trust
context: A guess x drawn from the draft distribution q is accepted outright when q(x) is at most p(x), the target's probability for it. Otherwise it is kept with probability p(x) divided by q(x). When a guess is rejected, the replacement is drawn not from p but from the adjusted distribution: p minus q, clipped at zero and renormalized. Accepting where the draft under-claims, thinning where it over-claims, and filling the rejected mass with exactly what the target wanted and the draft did not supply makes each output token distributed exactly as if the target had sampled it alone. The rule needs nothing from the draft except its probabilities, so the draft can be any model, even a bigram table. With temperature zero both distributions are one-hot and the rule reduces to keeping a guess exactly when the two models' argmax agree.

question: Why accept a guess with probability p(x)/q(x) when the draft over-claims it, rather than always accepting the draft's likely tokens?
choices: It keeps the draft from drifting away from the target
It cuts tokens the draft over-claims down to the target's rate
It saves target compute on the draft's confident guesses
explanation: A token proposed with probability q(x) and kept with probability p(x)/q(x) comes out with probability p(x), which is exactly the target's rate for it.

question: What would go wrong if a rejected guess were replaced by a plain sample from the target's distribution p?
choices: The output would no longer be distributed as the target's
Rejections would happen more often than they need to
The draft could never be rejected twice in a row
explanation: Accepted guesses already account for the mass where the draft under-claims; sampling the rest from p would count that mass twice, so the replacement must come from the residual p minus q.

title: Any draft will do
question: Why does the exactness guarantee hold for any draft, even a bigram table?
choices: The rule reads only the draft's probabilities
A weak draft is rejected on every guess, so the target decides
The target re-scores the draft before trusting it
explanation: The proof uses nothing about how q was produced, only its values; a poor draft lowers the acceptance rate and the speedup, never the correctness of the output.

title: The greedy case
question: With temperature zero, when is a draft guess kept?
choices: Exactly when the two models' argmax agree
Whenever the target gives it any probability at all
Always; greedy decoding has nothing to reject
explanation: At temperature zero both p and q are one-hot, so p(x)/q(x) is one when the argmaxes match and zero otherwise, and the method degrades to plain argmax decoding with lookahead.

question: What single property of the draft determines how many tokens an iteration yields on average?
choices: How often the target accepts its guesses
How many parameters it has relative to the target
How fast it runs relative to the target
explanation: The paper calls it alpha, the expected acceptance probability; tokens per iteration depend on alpha and gamma alone, while the draft's speed enters only the wall-clock cost.

title: More arithmetic per token
context: The method trades arithmetic for latency. An iteration does the work of gamma plus one target positions and gamma draft steps but yields fewer tokens than that on average, so total compute per token rises; the wall-clock gain exists only while the hardware has arithmetic to spare, which is the memory-bound regime of small batches. Two numbers govern the gain: the acceptance rate alpha, the probability that the target accepts a draft guess, and the cost coefficient c, the draft step's time as a fraction of the target's. The expected tokens per iteration is (1 - alpha^(gamma+1)) / (1 - alpha), and the expected speedup divides that by gamma c + 1. The draft and target must share a vocabulary. The best gamma depends on alpha and c: a better draft rewards longer speculation, a costlier draft punishes it.
question: Why does speculative decoding spend more arithmetic per token than plain decoding, even though it is faster?
choices: The draft recomputes the whole prefix on every iteration
The acceptance test runs over the entire vocabulary
Rejected positions were computed by the target and thrown away
explanation: The target evaluates gamma plus one positions each iteration but keeps fewer on average, and the draft's steps are extra; the method buys latency with compute that was idle anyway.

question: Why not always speculate with a very large gamma?
choices: Longer runs make the acceptance test inexact
The target can verify only a fixed number of positions
Late guesses rarely survive but still cost draft steps
explanation: The chance that guess k survives falls like alpha to the k, so past some point each extra draft step adds cost and almost no tokens; the optimal gamma rises with alpha and falls with c.

title: Same tokenizer
question: Why must the draft share the target's tokenizer?
choices: Different vocabularies would need two prompts
The draft writes directly into the target's KV cache
Acceptance compares both models' probability of one token
explanation: The rule compares p(x) and q(x) for the same symbol x, which only means something when both models speak the same vocabulary.

title: A slow draft
question: The draft is nearly as slow as the target, so c is close to one. What follows?
choices: The method becomes exact only in this regime
The gain is unchanged as long as alpha stays high
Little or no gain: drafting costs about what it saves
explanation: The speedup is the tokens per iteration divided by gamma c + 1; with c near one the gamma draft steps cost as much as gamma target steps would have.

title: No quality metric needed
context: The paper measures on T5-XXL, an eleven-billion-parameter encoder-decoder, with the small members of the same family as drafts, on English-to-German translation and on summarization, with greedy decoding and with sampling at temperature one. No model is retrained and the outputs are the target's own. Wall-clock speedups fall between two and three and a half times, higher for greedy decoding than for sampling and higher on translation than on summarization. A tiny GPT-like model with a bigram table as its draft also gains, modestly. The gains are on hardware that was memory-bound for the target alone.
question: Why can the paper report speedups without reporting any quality metric?
choices: The outputs are distributed exactly as the target's own
Translation metrics are too noisy to show a change
Quality was measured and found slightly higher
explanation: Exactness is proved, not measured: with the same seed the decoded text is the target's, so only wall-clock time is left to compare.

title: Greedy gains more
question: Why is the speedup larger for greedy decoding than for sampling at temperature one?
choices: Sampling forces the paper to use a smaller gamma
Argmax agreement is more likely than a sampled match
Greedy decoding skips the acceptance test entirely
explanation: With temperature the two models must draw the same token from spread-out distributions, which happens less often than their argmaxes coinciding, so alpha and the yield are lower.

title: Translation versus summarization
question: Why would translation gain more than summarization?
choices: Translation outputs are shorter, so fewer iterations
Summarization needs a larger vocabulary
The draft agrees with the target more often there
explanation: A more constrained task leaves fewer plausible next tokens, so a small model matches the large one more often and alpha is higher.

title: Even a bigram helps
question: Even a bigram table as draft gave a small speedup. What does that show?
choices: The target was weaker than expected on that data
Small transformers are unnecessary as drafts
Any guesser with the right vocabulary helps if cheap
explanation: A draft that costs almost nothing has c near zero, so even a low acceptance rate pays; the method is a framework for spending idle compute, not a particular small model.

title: Medusa
context: The acceptance rule became the standard way to make speculative methods exact, and later work changed only where the guesses come from. Medusa grows extra heads on the target to guess several positions without a second model; EAGLE drafts from the target's hidden features instead of its tokens; tree-structured verification checks several candidate continuations in one target pass. Production engines adopted it: Splash's DFlash draft proposes seven tokens per cycle and the target verifies eight rows in one pass, keeping the min(1, p/q) acceptance. The limit the paper named stayed: once serving is compute-bound, the free parallel slots are gone.
question: Medusa keeps the target but drops the separate draft model. What did it keep from this paper?
choices: A draft trained on the target's own outputs
One target pass over many guesses, exact acceptance
Guessing from a bigram table of the prompt
explanation: Later methods change only where guesses come from, here extra heads on the target; the verify-in-one-pass step and the acceptance rule are this paper's.

title: Drafting from features
question: Why might drafting from the target's hidden features beat drafting from its tokens?
choices: Features are cheaper to store than tokens
Token drafts cannot use the KV cache
Features carry what sampling a token threw away
explanation: A sampled token is one draw from a whole distribution; the hidden state behind it still holds the alternatives, so a draft fed with it guesses more like the target.

title: Trees of candidates
question: Why verify a tree of candidate continuations rather than one chain?
choices: More ways to be right per target pass, at compute cost
A single chain cannot be verified in one pass
Trees make the acceptance rule unnecessary
explanation: A pass over more positions is still nearly free while memory-bound, so checking several branches raises the expected accepted length for the same target call.

question: Why do throughput-oriented servers with huge batches rarely use speculative decoding?
choices: Their GPUs are compute-bound; nothing is idle
Large batches make acceptance rates fall
Drafts cannot be batched across requests
explanation: The method converts idle arithmetic into latency; a saturated GPU has none to convert, and the extra positions then cost real time.
